candidates.title: Why flamingos rest on one leg
candidates.opening_promise: Two clues to why flamingos rest on one leg.

thumbnail.concept: flamingo asleep on one leg on a force plate, sway marks either side

candidates.description: In 2017, a dead flamingo propped on one leg held steady with no muscle working. A 2010 zoo study found more birds did it in water and in the cold, which may save heat.
candidates.rationale: the viewer's own question, answered by two studies

candidates.title: A dead flamingo held steady on one leg
candidates.opening_promise: Why rest on one leg? A dead flamingo showed it.

thumbnail.concept: X-eyed flamingo on one leg on a lab bench, a check mark beside it

candidates.description: In a 2017 study, a dead flamingo held upright settled into a stable one-legged pose with no muscle activity, but would not stay steady on two legs.

candidates.title: One leg in cold water may save heat
candidates.opening_promise: Resting on one leg may also keep a flamingo warm.

thumbnail.concept: flamingo on one leg in water beside a cold thermometer

candidates.description: A 2010 zoo study found more flamingos rested on one leg in water than on land, and fewer as it got warmer, which suggests the pose helps keep heat.
candidates.rationale: the second, hedged reason as its own angle
